items.title: I can identify the key structural components of a neuron and describe their roles in transmitting information
items.what: A neuron has dendrites that receive incoming neuronal messages, an axon that transmits messages away from the cell body, axon terminals that send messages to the next neuron, and myelin that insulates the axon to prevent interference from other neurons.
items.why: Understanding neuron structure is essential for explaining how neuroplasticity works at a cellular level, including how new synapses form and how existing ones are modified.
items.example: When you first learn a piano scale, the dendrites of neurons involved in finger movement receive signals, the axon carries the message, and the axon terminals release it across the synapse to the next neuron. Over time, with practice, this pathway becomes faster because myelin thickens around the axon.

subtopic.name: The Neuron and Neuroplasticity
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces neurons as the structural units of the nervous system and defines neuroplasticity as the brain's ability to change in response to experience and environmental stimulation. It establishes the biological foundation needed to understand how and why the brain changes throughout life.
subtopic.why: Without understanding the neuron and what neuroplasticity means, it is impossible to explain how learning, development, or recovery from brain injury occurs. These concepts underpin all subsequent content in this chapter.

items.title: I can define the synapse and explain how neuronal messages cross the synaptic gap
items.what: The synapse is the region that includes the axon terminals of the presynaptic neuron, the synaptic gap, and the dendrites of the postsynaptic neuron. The presynaptic neuron fires a message across the synaptic gap, which the postsynaptic neuron receives.
items.why: Synaptic communication is the mechanism through which all neuroplastic changes occur. New synapses form, existing ones strengthen, and unused ones are eliminated — all at this junction.
items.example: When a student hears a new vocabulary word in French, the presynaptic neuron in the language processing region fires a message across the synaptic gap to the postsynaptic neuron, beginning the process of storing that word in memory.

It establishes the biological foundation needed to understand how and why the brain changes throughout life.
subtopic.why: Without understanding the neuron and what neuroplasticity means, it is impossible to explain how learning, development, or recovery from brain injury occurs. These concepts underpin all subsequent content in this chapter.

items.title: I can define neuroplasticity and distinguish between its two main types
items.what: Neuroplasticity is the ability of the brain to change in response to experience or environmental stimulation. It occurs as two types: developmental plasticity, which occurs in response to ageing and maturation, and adaptive plasticity, which occurs in response to new experiences, learning, or brain trauma.
items.why: Distinguishing between these two types allows students to correctly apply the concept to different scenarios — for example, a child learning to walk (developmental) versus a stroke patient relearning movement (adaptive).
items.example: A toddler forming new neural connections while learning to speak is an example of developmental plasticity. An adult relearning to use their right hand after a stroke damages the relevant motor cortex region is an example of adaptive plasticity.

subtopic.name: The Neuron and Neuroplasticity
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces neurons as the structural units of the nervous system and defines neuroplasticity as the brain's ability to change in response to experience and environmental stimulation. It establishes the biological foundation needed to understand how and why the brain changes throughout life.
subtopic.why: Without understanding the neuron and what neuroplasticity means, it is impossible to explain how learning, development, or recovery from brain injury occurs. These concepts underpin all subsequent content in this chapter.

items.title: I can define developmental plasticity and explain what triggers it
items.what: Developmental plasticity refers to changes in the brain that occur in response to ageing and maturation. It is driven by everyday learning experiences and the biological unfolding of development across the lifespan.
items.why: Recognising that developmental plasticity is a normal, ongoing process helps explain why children's brains are shaped so strongly by their early environments and experiences.
items.example: A child who is read to every night will develop stronger language-related neural networks than a child who receives little verbal stimulation, because repeated exposure drives synapse formation in language areas of the brain.

subtopic.name: Developmental Plasticity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how the brain changes structurally in response to ageing and maturation, with a focus on three processes: synaptogenesis, synaptic pruning, and myelination. It also examines the distinct neuroplastic trends observed during infancy and adolescence.
subtopic.why: Developmental plasticity explains why certain life stages are particularly sensitive to learning and why some skills are easier to acquire at certain ages than others. It connects neuroscience to observed patterns of cognitive and social development.

items.title: I can define synaptogenesis and explain when it is most intense
items.what: Synaptogenesis is the formation of synapses between neurons as axon terminals and dendrites grow toward one another. It occurs throughout the lifespan but is most intense during infancy, when there is a large volume of new information to encode.
items.why: Synaptogenesis is the mechanism by which the brain physically represents new learning. Understanding its timing explains why infant brains grow so rapidly in connectivity during the first years of life.
items.example: Between birth and age two or three, an infant's synaptic density in some cortical regions more than doubles compared to what an adult has. This reflects the enormous volume of synaptogenesis occurring as the infant learns to process language, movement, and social cues.

subtopic.name: Developmental Plasticity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how the brain changes structurally in response to ageing and maturation, with a focus on three processes: synaptogenesis, synaptic pruning, and myelination. It also examines the distinct neuroplastic trends observed during infancy and adolescence.
subtopic.why: Developmental plasticity explains why certain life stages are particularly sensitive to learning and why some skills are easier to acquire at certain ages than others. It connects neuroscience to observed patterns of cognitive and social development.

items.title: I can define synaptic pruning and explain why it is beneficial
items.what: Synaptic pruning is the elimination of underused synapses. Rather than losing capacity, the brain becomes more efficient by cutting weak connections so that the remaining, frequently used synapses are strengthened. The most intense periods of pruning occur in late infancy and adolescence.
items.why: Without pruning, the brain would maintain a vast number of weak, inefficient connections. Pruning ensures that the neural circuits the brain actually uses are fast and strong, which is essential for higher-order thinking in adolescence and adulthood.
items.example: A child who stops learning a second language by age four may have those specific language synapses pruned away. By adolescence, starting that language again is harder because the neural pathways are no longer there and must be rebuilt from scratch.

subtopic.name: Developmental Plasticity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how the brain changes structurally in response to ageing and maturation, with a focus on three processes: synaptogenesis, synaptic pruning, and myelination. It also examines the distinct neuroplastic trends observed during infancy and adolescence.
subtopic.why: Developmental plasticity explains why certain life stages are particularly sensitive to learning and why some skills are easier to acquire at certain ages than others. It connects neuroscience to observed patterns of cognitive and social development.

items.title: I can define myelination and explain its role across development
items.what: Myelination is the formation and development of myelin — a fatty sheath — around the axon of a neuron. Myelin insulates the neuron, speeds up signal transmission, and prevents interference from neighbouring neurons. It begins before birth and continues into early adulthood.
items.why: Myelination is what makes neural communication fast and reliable. Without it, the complex, interconnected thinking required in adolescence and adulthood would be slow and error-prone.
items.example: A child learning to ride a bike repeatedly practises until the movements feel automatic. This automaticity reflects myelination of the relevant motor pathways — the signals travel so efficiently that the skill no longer requires conscious effort.

subtopic.name: Developmental Plasticity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how the brain changes structurally in response to ageing and maturation, with a focus on three processes: synaptogenesis, synaptic pruning, and myelination. It also examines the distinct neuroplastic trends observed during infancy and adolescence.
subtopic.why: Developmental plasticity explains why certain life stages are particularly sensitive to learning and why some skills are easier to acquire at certain ages than others. It connects neuroscience to observed patterns of cognitive and social development.

items.title: I can compare the neuroplastic trends in infancy and adolescence
items.what: During infancy, there is a rapid increase in synaptic density driven by synaptogenesis, as the brain needs to form the foundations for many new skills. During adolescence, synaptic pruning is at its most intense, refining the brain's connections to support goal-directed, higher-order thinking.
items.why: Understanding these contrasting trends explains why infants can acquire skills like language with remarkable ease, while adolescents are better suited to deepening existing knowledge rather than forming entirely new neural foundations.
items.example: A two-year-old has a synaptic density more than double that of an adult in some brain areas. By late adolescence, extensive pruning has reduced this density, but the remaining synapses are far more efficient and myelinated, supporting complex reasoning.

subtopic.name: Developmental Plasticity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how the brain changes structurally in response to ageing and maturation, with a focus on three processes: synaptogenesis, synaptic pruning, and myelination. It also examines the distinct neuroplastic trends observed during infancy and adolescence.
subtopic.why: Developmental plasticity explains why certain life stages are particularly sensitive to learning and why some skills are easier to acquire at certain ages than others. It connects neuroscience to observed patterns of cognitive and social development.

items.title: I can define adaptive plasticity and identify the two situations in which it occurs
items.what: Adaptive plasticity is the brain's ability to change its structure and function in response to new experiences, learning, and environmental demands, as well as to compensate for injury. It occurs in response to both everyday learning demands and damage caused by brain trauma.
items.why: Adaptive plasticity is the mechanism behind rehabilitation after brain injury. Recognising that it can occur in healthy brains as well as injured ones helps explain why practice and learning continue to physically change the brain throughout life.
items.example: A professional musician who practises daily is using adaptive plasticity — the motor and auditory areas of their brain become larger and more densely connected over time. An AFL player recovering from a stroke uses adaptive plasticity to rebuild lost motor function.

subtopic.name: Adaptive Plasticity and Maintaining Brain Function
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how the brain adapts its structure and function in response to injury and new experiences through sprouting and rerouting. It also covers evidence-based strategies for maintaining and maximising brain functioning across the lifespan.
subtopic.why: Adaptive plasticity explains how people can recover function after brain injury and why rehabilitation is possible. The strategies for maintaining brain function have direct, practical application to students' own lives and the lives of people with neurological conditions.

items.title: I can define sprouting and explain how it helps the brain recover from trauma
items.what: Sprouting is the ability of a neuron to develop new branches on its dendrites or axons. After brain trauma, these new branches extend the neuron's reach, allowing it to form new connections in areas where neural activity has been disrupted.
items.why: Sprouting is one of the key mechanisms by which the brain physically repairs itself after injury. Without it, neurons damaged by trauma would be permanently isolated, with no way to re-establish communication with other brain regions.
items.example: After Emilia Clarke suffered two brain aneurysms that caused brain tissue damage, her neurons may have undergone sprouting — growing new axon or dendrite branches to reach undamaged tissue nearby, enabling her to regain normal functioning.

subtopic.name: Adaptive Plasticity and Maintaining Brain Function
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how the brain adapts its structure and function in response to injury and new experiences through sprouting and rerouting. It also covers evidence-based strategies for maintaining and maximising brain functioning across the lifespan.
subtopic.why: Adaptive plasticity explains how people can recover function after brain injury and why rehabilitation is possible. The strategies for maintaining brain function have direct, practical application to students' own lives and the lives of people with neurological conditions.

items.title: I can define rerouting and explain how it differs from sprouting
items.what: Rerouting is a neuron's ability to abandon its connection with a damaged neuron and form a new synaptic connection with an undamaged neuron instead. Unlike sprouting, which involves growing new branches from a damaged neuron, rerouting involves an undamaged neuron seeking a healthier partner.
items.why: Rerouting allows the brain to work around damaged areas rather than waiting for those areas to recover. This is why some people can regain functions they appeared to have permanently lost after a brain injury.
items.example: A physiotherapy patient who suffered a traumatic brain injury practises hand exercises daily. Over weeks, neurons previously connected to the damaged motor region reroute to connect with neighbouring undamaged neurons, gradually restoring hand movement.

subtopic.name: Adaptive Plasticity and Maintaining Brain Function
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how the brain adapts its structure and function in response to injury and new experiences through sprouting and rerouting. It also covers evidence-based strategies for maintaining and maximising brain functioning across the lifespan.
subtopic.why: Adaptive plasticity explains how people can recover function after brain injury and why rehabilitation is possible. The strategies for maintaining brain function have direct, practical application to students' own lives and the lives of people with neurological conditions.

items.title: I can identify and explain four evidence-based ways to maintain or maximise brain functioning
items.what: Research supports four main strategies: mental stimulation (such as puzzles or learning an instrument), a balanced diet (particularly foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids and vitamin K), regular physical activity (at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity per day for young people), and social support (regular interaction with others).
items.why: Each of these strategies has a distinct neurobiological mechanism. Knowing why they work — not just that they work — allows students to evaluate claims about brain health and apply the strategies meaningfully.
items.example: Physical activity increases blood flow to the brain and promotes the growth of new neurons in the hippocampus, the brain region central to learning and memory. A student who jogs three times a week is supporting their memory capacity, not just their cardiovascular fitness.

subtopic.name: Adaptive Plasticity and Maintaining Brain Function
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how the brain adapts its structure and function in response to injury and new experiences through sprouting and rerouting. It also covers evidence-based strategies for maintaining and maximising brain functioning across the lifespan.
subtopic.why: Adaptive plasticity explains how people can recover function after brain injury and why rehabilitation is possible. The strategies for maintaining brain function have direct, practical application to students' own lives and the lives of people with neurological conditions.

items.title: I can define acquired brain injury and distinguish between traumatic and non-traumatic types
items.what: An acquired brain injury refers to all types of brain injury that occur after birth. Traumatic brain injuries are caused by an external force (such as a fall or sports collision), while non-traumatic brain injuries are caused by internal factors (such as a stroke, tumour, or aneurysm).
items.why: The distinction between traumatic and non-traumatic injury is important because it determines how the injury is classified, what caused it, and in some cases, how it might be prevented or treated.
items.example: Catherine, who was injured in a motor vehicle accident, sustained a traumatic brain injury because the damage was caused by an external force. Her mother, who had a stroke, sustained a non-traumatic brain injury because the damage was caused by internal disruption to blood flow.

subtopic.name: Acquired Brain Injury and Its Impacts
subtopic.what: This subtopic defines acquired brain injury as an umbrella term for all brain injuries occurring after birth, distinguishes between traumatic and non-traumatic types, and examines the impact of such injuries on biological, psychological, and social functioning.
subtopic.why: Brain injuries are relatively common and have profound, wide-ranging consequences. Understanding the biopsychosocial model of impact helps students appreciate why recovery is complex and why no two brain injuries produce identical outcomes.

items.title: I can explain why the effects of acquired brain injury vary between individuals
items.what: The effects of a brain injury differ between individuals in the rate at which symptoms develop, their intensity, and their duration. Impairments can be permanent or temporary and may be specific or widespread, depending on which brain region is damaged.
items.why: Recognising individual variability prevents overgeneralisation and reminds students that brain injuries must be assessed and treated on a case-by-case basis.
items.example: Two people who both suffer strokes may have very different outcomes. One may show mild symptoms that resolve within weeks, while the other may experience severe, lasting impairment — even if both experienced a stroke in a similar brain region.

subtopic.name: Acquired Brain Injury and Its Impacts
subtopic.what: This subtopic defines acquired brain injury as an umbrella term for all brain injuries occurring after birth, distinguishes between traumatic and non-traumatic types, and examines the impact of such injuries on biological, psychological, and social functioning.
subtopic.why: Brain injuries are relatively common and have profound, wide-ranging consequences. Understanding the biopsychosocial model of impact helps students appreciate why recovery is complex and why no two brain injuries produce identical outcomes.

items.title: I can explain how acquired brain injury affects biological functioning, using specific examples
items.what: Biological functioning encompasses behaviour, organ function, and cellular and neuronal function. Acquired brain injury can cause seizures (due to abnormal electrical disturbances from scar tissue), movement impairment (paralysis from disrupted motor signals), and smell impairment (from damage to olfactory neuronal pathways).
items.why: Biological impacts are often the most immediately visible consequences of brain injury and can dramatically affect a person's independence and quality of life.
items.example: A person who sustains damage to the motor cortex may develop paralysis in the contralateral limbs, because the brain can no longer send adequate motor neural messages to those skeletal muscles to initiate movement.

subtopic.name: Acquired Brain Injury and Its Impacts
subtopic.what: This subtopic defines acquired brain injury as an umbrella term for all brain injuries occurring after birth, distinguishes between traumatic and non-traumatic types, and examines the impact of such injuries on biological, psychological, and social functioning.
subtopic.why: Brain injuries are relatively common and have profound, wide-ranging consequences. Understanding the biopsychosocial model of impact helps students appreciate why recovery is complex and why no two brain injuries produce identical outcomes.

items.title: I can explain how acquired brain injury affects psychological functioning, using specific examples
items.what: Psychological functioning encompasses cognition, behaviour, and emotion. Acquired brain injury can cause memory loss (from hippocampal damage), personality changes (including impulsivity, irritability, and emotional instability), and increased susceptibility to mental health disorders such as anxiety and mood disorders.
items.why: Psychological impacts of brain injury are often less visible than physical ones but can be equally or more debilitating, affecting the person's sense of self, their relationships, and their ability to work.
items.example: Following a traumatic brain injury, a formerly calm and methodical engineer may become impulsive and emotionally volatile due to damage to the prefrontal cortex, the region responsible for regulating behaviour and complex decision-making.

subtopic.name: Acquired Brain Injury and Its Impacts
subtopic.what: This subtopic defines acquired brain injury as an umbrella term for all brain injuries occurring after birth, distinguishes between traumatic and non-traumatic types, and examines the impact of such injuries on biological, psychological, and social functioning.
subtopic.why: Brain injuries are relatively common and have profound, wide-ranging consequences. Understanding the biopsychosocial model of impact helps students appreciate why recovery is complex and why no two brain injuries produce identical outcomes.

items.title: I can explain how acquired brain injury affects social functioning, using specific examples
items.what: Social functioning encompasses relationships, interactions with the environment, and interpersonal skills. Acquired brain injury can reduce job productivity (through reduced concentration, physical limitations, or fatigue), strain social relationships (leading to withdrawal or difficulty maintaining connections), and increase antisocial behaviour (through lowered self-esteem and increased aggression).
items.why: Social impacts reflect how brain injury ripples outward into a person's everyday life and community. They are often the most persistent long-term consequences of injury.
items.example: Catherine, after her motor vehicle accident, experienced a marriage breakdown and had to move back with her mother — both direct social consequences of the functional limitations and relationship strain caused by her traumatic brain injury.

subtopic.name: Acquired Brain Injury and Its Impacts
subtopic.what: This subtopic defines acquired brain injury as an umbrella term for all brain injuries occurring after birth, distinguishes between traumatic and non-traumatic types, and examines the impact of such injuries on biological, psychological, and social functioning.
subtopic.why: Brain injuries are relatively common and have profound, wide-ranging consequences. Understanding the biopsychosocial model of impact helps students appreciate why recovery is complex and why no two brain injuries produce identical outcomes.

items.title: I can define neurological disorders and explain why they are difficult to study
items.what: Neurological disorders are diseases characterised by damage to or malfunctioning of the nervous system. They are difficult to study because the brain is uniquely complex, causes can range from genetics and lifestyle to toxins and injury, and environmental variables are constantly changing.
items.why: Understanding the challenges of studying neurological disorders helps students evaluate contemporary research with appropriate scepticism and appreciate why many findings remain preliminary.
items.example: Epilepsy was historically misattributed to supernatural causes and Parkinson's disease was classified purely by its symptoms for decades, with little understanding of its neurochemical basis — illustrating how difficult it is to understand these conditions even with sustained scientific effort.

subtopic.name: Neurological Disorders and Contemporary Research
subtopic.what: This subtopic defines neurological disorders and focuses on two key examples — Parkinson's disease and epilepsy — before examining how contemporary research using machine learning and the gut-brain axis is improving understanding and treatment of these conditions.
subtopic.why: Contemporary research is actively reshaping what we know about neurological disorders. Evaluating this research critically helps students understand both the promise and the limitations of emerging findings in psychology and neuroscience.

items.title: I can describe the key features of Parkinson's disease, including its neurochemical basis
items.what: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disease caused by the loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain. Dopamine is the neurotransmitter responsible for coordinating voluntary movement and the experience of pleasure and pain. Symptoms include tremors, reduced motor control, muscle stiffness, fatigue, depression, and anxiety.
items.why: Parkinson's disease is one of the most common neurodegenerative conditions and its neurochemical basis — dopamine loss — links directly to concepts students already know about neurotransmission and brain function.
items.example: As dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra are progressively lost, a person with Parkinson's disease begins to lose fine motor control. This is why a tremor at rest — the hand shaking when doing nothing — is one of the earliest observable signs of the disease.

subtopic.name: Neurological Disorders and Contemporary Research
subtopic.what: This subtopic defines neurological disorders and focuses on two key examples — Parkinson's disease and epilepsy — before examining how contemporary research using machine learning and the gut-brain axis is improving understanding and treatment of these conditions.
subtopic.why: Contemporary research is actively reshaping what we know about neurological disorders. Evaluating this research critically helps students understand both the promise and the limitations of emerging findings in psychology and neuroscience.

items.title: I can describe the key features of epilepsy, including the process of epileptogenesis
items.what: Epilepsy is a neurological disorder characterised by abnormal electrical activity in the brain and recurrent, unprovoked seizures. Epileptogenesis is the process during which structural and functional changes occur in the brain, creating an environment that supports seizures. Seizures themselves are brief episodes of uncontrolled electrical discharging of neurons.
items.why: Understanding epileptogenesis shifts the focus from the seizure itself (the symptom) to the underlying brain changes that make seizures possible — which is where treatment and prevention efforts are increasingly directed.
items.example: A person who has suffered a traumatic brain injury may not develop epilepsy immediately. Epileptogenesis is the gradual process of neural reorganisation after the injury that eventually creates the conditions for recurrent seizures to begin, sometimes months or years later.

subtopic.name: Neurological Disorders and Contemporary Research
subtopic.what: This subtopic defines neurological disorders and focuses on two key examples — Parkinson's disease and epilepsy — before examining how contemporary research using machine learning and the gut-brain axis is improving understanding and treatment of these conditions.
subtopic.why: Contemporary research is actively reshaping what we know about neurological disorders. Evaluating this research critically helps students understand both the promise and the limitations of emerging findings in psychology and neuroscience.

items.title: I can explain how machine learning is used to improve the diagnosis of neurological disorders
items.what: Machine learning is an element of artificial intelligence that uses algorithms trained on large datasets to classify information and make predictions. Supervised learning uses labelled data (such as brain scans labelled as Parkinson's-affected or typical) to diagnose disorders. Unsupervised learning analyses unlabelled data to identify previously unrecognised patterns, such as demographic risk factors.
items.why: Machine learning can analyse data at a scale and speed that is impossible for human clinicians, potentially identifying disorders earlier and more accurately. Comparing its diagnostic accuracy to traditional methods helps students evaluate the significance of this research.
items.example: A meta-analysis found that machine learning analysing multiple data types (such as voice, movement, and MRI) achieved a combined diagnostic accuracy of around 92.6% for Parkinson's disease, compared to 73.8–83.9% accuracy for traditional clinical diagnosis.

subtopic.name: Neurological Disorders and Contemporary Research
subtopic.what: This subtopic defines neurological disorders and focuses on two key examples — Parkinson's disease and epilepsy — before examining how contemporary research using machine learning and the gut-brain axis is improving understanding and treatment of these conditions.
subtopic.why: Contemporary research is actively reshaping what we know about neurological disorders. Evaluating this research critically helps students understand both the promise and the limitations of emerging findings in psychology and neuroscience.

items.title: I can explain what the gut-brain axis is and describe relevant research findings for Parkinson's disease and epilepsy
items.what: The gut-brain axis refers to the bidirectional connection between the gut and the brain through multiple parts of the nervous system. The gut can influence neurochemical and behavioural changes in the brain, while the brain can influence gut functioning. Imbalanced gut microbiota has been linked to the progression of neurological disorders.
items.why: The gut-brain axis represents a genuinely new direction in understanding and potentially treating neurological disorders. It challenges the assumption that the brain is the sole driver of neurological conditions.
items.example: Research suggests Parkinson's disease may begin in the gut — constipation is among the earliest symptoms in up to 50% of patients and often precedes motor symptoms by years. Separately, providing epilepsy patients with probiotics has been associated with up to a 50% reduction in seizure frequency in some studies.

subtopic.name: Neurological Disorders and Contemporary Research
subtopic.what: This subtopic defines neurological disorders and focuses on two key examples — Parkinson's disease and epilepsy — before examining how contemporary research using machine learning and the gut-brain axis is improving understanding and treatment of these conditions.
subtopic.why: Contemporary research is actively reshaping what we know about neurological disorders. Evaluating this research critically helps students understand both the promise and the limitations of emerging findings in psychology and neuroscience.

items.title: I can evaluate why contemporary research on neurological disorders should be interpreted cautiously
items.what: Contemporary research has not always undergone the full scrutiny of older, well-established research. In particular, replication — where independent researchers reproduce a study to test its reliability — is often limited for very recent findings. This means conclusions may shift as more evidence accumulates.
items.why: Critical evaluation of research quality is a core science skill. Understanding that emerging research is valuable but provisional helps students avoid overstating conclusions and prepares them to assess new findings in future.
items.example: Studies suggesting probiotic and antibiotic treatments for epilepsy may rival traditional drug treatments are promising, but many have compromised study designs and have not been independently replicated. The finding is noteworthy but not yet sufficient to change clinical practice.

items.title: I can define CTE and explain why it is classified as a neurodegenerative disease
items.what: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a progressive and fatal brain disease associated with repeated head injuries and concussions. It is classified as a neurodegenerative disease because neurons are progressively lost over time and brain functioning worsens gradually rather than all at once.
items.why: The neurodegenerative classification distinguishes CTE from acute brain injury — the damage is not immediate but accumulates slowly, which is why symptoms often appear years or decades after the original injuries.
items.example: An AFL player who suffered repeated concussions during their playing career in their 20s may not display obvious symptoms until their 30s or 40s. The brain has been progressively degenerating throughout that time, even when the person appeared to be functioning normally.

subtopic.name: Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE)
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) as an example of emerging research into progressive and fatal brain disease, covering its causes, symptoms, neurological mechanisms, diagnostic limitations, and the history of research into the condition.
subtopic.why: CTE has significant real-world relevance, particularly in contact sports such as AFL, NRL, and boxing. It illustrates how emerging psychological research can directly shape sporting regulations, public health policy, and individual decision-making.

items.title: I can identify the common causes of CTE and the populations most at risk
items.what: CTE is typically caused by repeated concussions — mild traumatic brain injuries that temporarily disrupt brain function. It is most commonly associated with contact sports (such as boxing, AFL, NRL, and American football), combat in military service, and intimate partner violence. Research also suggests a single severe traumatic brain injury can, in some cases, trigger CTE.
items.why: Identifying at-risk populations is important for prevention, early awareness, and the design of protective regulations in sport and military settings.
items.example: Over an 8-year period, 8,905 concussions were reported from community football in Australia alone. The cumulative risk from repeated concussions in community-level players — not just elite athletes — makes CTE a public health concern, not just a professional sport one.

subtopic.name: Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE)
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) as an example of emerging research into progressive and fatal brain disease, covering its causes, symptoms, neurological mechanisms, diagnostic limitations, and the history of research into the condition.
subtopic.why: CTE has significant real-world relevance, particularly in contact sports such as AFL, NRL, and boxing. It illustrates how emerging psychological research can directly shape sporting regulations, public health policy, and individual decision-making.

items.title: I can describe the symptoms of CTE and explain when they typically appear
items.what: CTE symptoms typically appear 8 to 10 years after the experience of repetitive concussions and are most commonly seen in older, retired athletes and war veterans. Symptoms include impaired executive functions (such as reasoning and decision-making), memory loss, depression, difficulties with attention, disturbances in behaviour, anxiety, paranoia, and mood impairments including increased aggression.
items.why: The delayed onset of symptoms — often decades after the causal injuries — is one of the most important and counterintuitive features of CTE. It means athletes and their families may not connect current symptoms to past sporting injuries.
items.example: Shane Tuck, a former AFL player, was 38 when he died. His family had noticed signs of depression and personality change prior to his death. These symptoms were consistent with Stage III–IV CTE, even though his playing career had ended years earlier.

subtopic.name: Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE)
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) as an example of emerging research into progressive and fatal brain disease, covering its causes, symptoms, neurological mechanisms, diagnostic limitations, and the history of research into the condition.
subtopic.why: CTE has significant real-world relevance, particularly in contact sports such as AFL, NRL, and boxing. It illustrates how emerging psychological research can directly shape sporting regulations, public health policy, and individual decision-making.

items.title: I can describe the four stages of CTE and how symptoms progress
items.what: CTE is described in four progressive stages. Stage I involves headaches and loss of attention. Stage II includes depression, mood swings, short-term memory loss, and emotional outbursts. Stage III involves executive dysfunction, sustained memory loss, and visuospatial difficulties. Stage IV involves dementia, profound cognitive decline, aggression, paranoia, language difficulties, and suicidal thoughts.
items.why: Understanding the staged progression helps explain why CTE is fatal — the degeneration is not static but worsening, and by Stage IV the brain has deteriorated to a point where sustaining normal life becomes impossible.
items.example: A retired boxer showing Stage II symptoms — irritability and short-term memory loss — may appear to have a manageable mental health issue. Without awareness of CTE, clinicians might treat the depression alone, missing the underlying neurodegenerative process driving it.

subtopic.name: Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE)
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) as an example of emerging research into progressive and fatal brain disease, covering its causes, symptoms, neurological mechanisms, diagnostic limitations, and the history of research into the condition.
subtopic.why: CTE has significant real-world relevance, particularly in contact sports such as AFL, NRL, and boxing. It illustrates how emerging psychological research can directly shape sporting regulations, public health policy, and individual decision-making.

items.title: I can explain the neurological mechanism underlying CTE, specifically the role of p-tau and neurofibrillary tangles
items.what: CTE is characterised by the widespread accumulation of a protein called p-tau (hyperphosphorylated tau) in brain regions including the brainstem, hippocampus, and cerebral cortex — particularly the frontal and temporal lobes. This protein forms neurofibrillary tangles inside neurons, which block the transport of essential substances within the neuron and eventually kill it.
items.why: Understanding the molecular mechanism of CTE connects its symptoms to specific brain regions and helps explain why CTE symptoms (such as memory loss and executive dysfunction) map onto the regions most affected.
items.example: Neuropathologist Michael Buckland, examining Shane Tuck's donated brain after his death, reported that the tau accumulation was so extensive he could see it without a microscope — an indication of the most severe form of CTE documented in an Australian footballer at that time.

items.title: I can explain why CTE can only be definitively diagnosed post-mortem
items.what: A conclusive diagnosis of CTE requires a post-mortem examination — an assessment of the brain after death — because current brain scanning technology cannot detect the p-tau accumulation and neurofibrillary tangles that define the disease. This means that during a person's lifetime, CTE can only be suspected, not confirmed.
items.why: The inability to diagnose CTE in living patients is one of the most significant limitations of current research and clinical practice. It complicates research design, prevents early intervention, and creates ethical challenges around consent and brain donation.
items.example: Desmond, a war veteran showing erratic decision-making and mood changes, cannot be diagnosed with CTE while he is alive — regardless of how convincingly his symptoms suggest it. A definitive diagnosis would require examination of his brain tissue after death.

items.title: I can outline the history of CTE research from 1928 to the present
items.what: CTE research began in 1928 when Martland described 'punch drunk syndrome' in boxers showing cognitive impairment from repeated blows. Research expanded significantly in 2005 with the first confirmed case in an American football player (Mike Webster). The VA-BU-CLF Brain Bank was established in 2008 and found CTE in approximately two-thirds of over 1,000 donated brains. The Australian Sports Brain Bank was established in 2018 and has since identified CTE in AFL and NRL players.
items.why: Tracing the history of CTE research illustrates how scientific understanding develops incrementally and shows students that what is now accepted as a serious public health concern was once unrecognised or dismissed.
items.example: Despite the first cases of 'punch drunk syndrome' being described in 1928, fewer than 50 cases were confirmed in the following 75 years. The exponential growth in CTE research since 2005 demonstrates how a single high-profile case — Mike Webster — can catalyse an entire field of scientific inquiry.

items.title: I can describe how CTE research has influenced sporting regulations and prevention strategies
items.what: CTE research has directly shaped policy responses. In the AFL, players diagnosed with concussion are now automatically stood down for 12 days, on-field concussion assessment protocols have been tightened, and the HeadCheck app has been developed for community clubs. Education and behavioural therapies have also been identified as helpful in managing persistent post-concussion symptoms. Currently, there is no cure for CTE.
items.why: The translation of emerging research into real-world policy is a key example of how psychology operates as a science with direct human consequences. It also demonstrates that research does not have to be complete to be useful — it can guide precautionary action even before definitive answers are available.
items.example: As of 2021, an AFL player diagnosed with concussion cannot return to training or competition for a minimum of 12 days — a rule that did not exist before CTE research made the cumulative risks of repeated concussion undeniable.
